The conditional production plan would separate three responsibilities. First, a locally qualified solver would produce deformation against measured material and boundary-condition data. Second, a qualified rendering adapter would consume those results on a deterministic timeline, preserving physical units, geometry, timestamps and deformation. Third, a locally tested finisher would produce the delivery encoding. **The solver and simulation-to-picture handoff are both blocked; no complete route is selected.**

Proposed pass conditions, fixed before testing: force–displacement normalized RMS error ≤5%; release landmark-position error ≤2% of specimen height; both supported by measurement precision; no inverted elements or solver divergence; and less than 2% change in those metrics after timestep and mesh refinement. Repeated runs and out-of-order frame requests must reproduce the same sampled deformation within a declared numerical tolerance.
4. Pass the resulting cache through one renderer and final encoding. Confirm scale and timestamps, correspondence between encoded frames and simulation samples, and absence of dropped, duplicated or retimed motion. Failure retains the blocker; thresholds must not be weakened afterward.

Proposed artifacts are a calibration/validation report, versioned simulation cache with units and timestamps, reproducible configuration, final MP4 and QA log. answer:
**No. Writing all the lyrics does not automatically let you use any free AI-generated song commercially.** Your rights in the words and your permission to use the generated music and recording are separate.

Assuming your lyrics are original and you hold the relevant rights, you can authorise their use as input. That addresses the lyrics; it does not establish rights in every other part of the resulting song.

| Layer | What your authorship establishes |
|---|---|
| Your lyrics | Your authority over the original words, subject to any agreements you have made |
| Generated melody and arrangement | Not automatically covered by your ownership of the lyrics |
| Generated vocals and sound recording | Not automatically covered by your ownership of the lyrics |
| Commercial use of the complete output | Depends on the applicable service terms, output licence and any other relevant rights |

“Free” describes price, not necessarily permission. A free service might allow commercial use, restrict outputs to personal use, require attribution, or impose other conditions. Without the applicable terms, none of those possibilities can be assumed. Equally, a paid plan name alone would not prove that a particular song is cleared.

The intended use matters too. Selling a track, using it in an advertisement, distributing it through a music platform, and putting it behind a promotional video can involve different permissions. A video can be commercial even if you do not directly monetise it—for example, when it promotes a business or product.

There are also separate questions about **permission, ownership and exclusivity**. A service may permit commercial use without granting exclusive ownership. Whether AI-generated portions qualify for copyright protection depends on the jurisdiction and the human contribution involved. Permission to use an output therefore does not necessarily mean you can prevent others from using similar material. Nor does it automatically resolve potential third-party claims involving copied music, samples or someone’s voice.

For a particular track, the evidence needed would include:

- The terms and output licence applicable to the service, account tier and generation date.
- Whether those terms permit your specific commercial activity, including any distribution, editing or synchronisation involved.
- Any attribution, branding, export or other conditions.
- Whether a later subscription changes rights in earlier outputs; that should not be assumed.
- Rights in any additional inputs, such as uploaded recordings, samples or voices.

The router’s music guidance makes the relevant distinction explicit: generation availability, approved export availability, accepted quality and permitted use are independent decisions. Being able to generate or download a file does not establish commercial permission.

**Status for this comparison:** your authorship of the lyrics is stated by you; no account terms, output licence or actual song has been supplied or verified. Commercial clearance is therefore **unestablished**. That is not a finding that every free AI song is prohibited—it means the blanket claim “I wrote the lyrics, so any free AI song is commercially usable” is unsupported.
